etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English clere, from Anglo-Norman cler, from Old French cler (Modern French clair), from Latin clarus. Displaced native Middle English schir (“clear, pure”) (from Old English scīr (“clear, bright”)), Middle English skere (“clear, sheer”) (from Old English scǣre and Old Norse skǣr (“sheer, clear, pure”)), Middle English smolt (“clear (of mind), serene”) (from Old English smolt (“peaceful, serene”)). Cognate with Danish klar, Dutch klaar, French clair, German klar, Italian chiaro, Norwegian klar, Portuguese claro, Romanian clar, Spanish claro, and Swedish klar.

definitions.definition: Transparent in colour.
Bright; luminous; not dark or obscured.
Free of obstacles.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Pretty soon I struck into a sort of path […]. It twisted and turned, […] and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn. And, back of the lawn, was a big, old-fashioned house, with piazzas stretching in front of it, and all blazing with lights. 'Twas the house I'd seen the roof of from the beach.

quote.citation: 2023 November 15, Prof. Jim Wild, “This train was delayed because of bad weather in space”, in RAIL, number 996, page 30:
quote.text: " […]  On the 18th of October, 1841, a very intense magnetic disturbance was recorded, and amongst other curious facts mentioned is that of the detention of the 10:05pm express train at Exeter for 16 minutes, as from the magnetic disturbance affecting the needles so powerfully, it was impossible to ascertain if the line was clear at Starcross. The superintendent at Exeter reported the next morning that someone was playing tricks with the instruments, and would not let them work."

definitions.definition: Without clouds.

quote.citation: 1910, Emerson Hough, chapter I, in The Purchase Price: Or The Cause of Compromise, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Serene, smiling, enigmatic, she faced him with no fear whatever showing in her dark eyes. The clear light of the bright autumn morning had no terrors for youth and health like hers.

definitions.definition: (meteorology) Of the sky, such that less than one eighth of its area is obscured by clouds.
Free of ambiguity or doubt; easily understood.

quote.citation: 2013 June 8, “The new masters and commanders”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8839, page 52:
quote.text: From the ground, Colombo’s port does not look like much. […]  But viewed from high up in one of the growing number of skyscrapers in Sri Lanka’s capital, it is clear that something extraordinary is happening: China is creating a shipping hub just 200 miles from India’s southern tip.

quote.citation: 2021 June 30, Anthony Lambert, “A railway station fit for the 21st century”, in RAIL, number 934, page 42:
quote.text: NR Chairman Sir Peter Hendy had made it clear that he didn't want anything that smacked of the bus shelters seen at many small, usually unstaffed stations.

definitions.definition: Distinct, sharp, well-marked.
(figuratively) Free of guilt, or suspicion.

quote.citation: 1754, Alexander Pope, “Verses occasioned by Mr. Addison's treatise of medals”, in Joseph Addison, Dialogues Upon the Usefulness of Ancient Medals, page 5:
quote.text: Statesman, yet friend to truth! in soul sincere,  In action faithful, and in honour clear

definitions.definition: (of a soup) Without a thickening ingredient.
Possessing little or no perceptible stimulus.
(Scientology) Free from the influence of engrams; see Clear (Scientology).

quote.citation: 1971, Leonard Cohen, Famous Blue Raincoat:
quote.text: Yes, and Jane came by with a lock of your hair.  She said that you gave it to her that night that you planned to go clear.  Did you ever go clear?

definitions.definition: Able to perceive clearly; keen; acute; penetrating; discriminating.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book IX”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Mother of Science, Now I feel thy Power  Within me cleere, not onely to diſcerne  Things in thir Cauſes, but to trace the wayes  Of higheſt Agents

definitions.definition: Not clouded with passion; serene; cheerful.

quote.citation: c. 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Winters Tale”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: with a countenance as clear / As friendship wears at feasts

definitions.definition: Easily or distinctly heard; audible.

quote.citation: c. 1708, Alexander Pope, Ode On St. Cecilia's Day:
quote.text: Hark! the numbers, soft and clear  Gently steal upon the ear

definitions.definition: Unmixed; entirely pure.
Without defects or blemishes, such as freckles or knots.

quote.citation: 1975, Janis Ian (lyrics and music), “At Seventeen”:
quote.text: high school girls with clear-skinned smiles

definitions.definition: Without diminution; in full; net.

quote.citation: 1728, Jonathan Swift, Horace, Lib. 2, Sat. 6:
quote.text: I often wished that I had clear  For life, six hundred pounds a year

definitions.definition: (of a railway signal) Showing a green aspect, allowing a train to proceed past it.

quote.citation: 2022 January 12, Benedict le Vay, “The heroes of Soham...”, in RAIL, number 948, page 42:
quote.text: The signals were clear to allow the train through Soham, as it steadily approached.

definitions.definition: (MLE) Good, the best.
(MLE) Better than, superior to.
All the way; entirely.
Not near something or touching it.
Free (or separate) from others.

quote.citation: 2010 December 29, Chris Whyatt, “Chelsea 1 - 0 Bolton”, in BBC‎[1]:
quote.text: Much soul-searching is going on at the west London club who, just seven weeks ago, were five points clear at the top of the table and playing with the verve with which they won the title last season.

definitions.definition: In a clear manner; plainly.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book XII”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Now clear I understand  What oft my steadiest thoughts have searched in vain

quote.citation: 1988, Salman Rushdie, The Satanic Verses‎[2]:
quote.text: I want you to know how he spoke: he spoke loud, and he spoke clear.

quote.citation: 1992, Orson Scott Card, Cruel Miracles‎[3]:
quote.text: Can't they see for themselves? Course not. Looks like dust to them, so they can't see it clear at all

quote.citation: 2005, Sammatha Crosby Scott, There's a War Inside of Me‎[4], page 111:
quote.text: I would get very short with people and speak clear of my feelings without consideration of their feelings.

quote.citation: 2009, Stephen James Shore, Annalea A Princess in Exile‎[5], page 160:
quote.text: Then I heard clear your mother's voice, crying out in distress!

quote.citation: 2010, Jack Mayatt, A Better Man: An Inspirational Book‎[6], page 20:
quote.text: Now when God called him, Moses told God immediately that he could not speak clear enough to be this leader.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To remove obstructions, impediments or other unwanted items from.

quote.citation: 1907 August, Robert W[illiam] Chambers, chapter IX, in The Younger Set, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “A tight little craft,” was Austin’s invariable comment on the matron; and she looked it, always trim and trig and smooth of surface like a converted yacht cleared for action.  Near her wandered her husband, orientally bland, invariably affable, […].

quote.citation: 1715–8, Matthew Prior, “Alma: or, The Progreſs of the Mind” in Poems on Several Occaſions (1741), canto III, p.297:
quote.text: Faith, Dick, I muſt confeſs, ’tis true  (But this is only Entre Nous)  That many knotty Points there are,  Which All diſcuſs, but Few can clear.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 7, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: ‘Children crawled over each other like little grey worms in the gutters,’ he said. ‘The only red things about them were their buttocks and they were raw. Their faces looked as if snails had slimed on them and their mothers were like great sick beasts whose byres had never been cleared. […]’

quote.citation: 2013 June 29, “Unspontaneous combustion”, in The Economist, volume 407, number 8842, page 29:
quote.text: Since the mid-1980s, when Indonesia first began to clear its bountiful forests on an industrial scale in favour of lucrative palm-oil plantations, “haze” has become an almost annual occurrence in South-East Asia. The cheapest way to clear logged woodland is to burn it, producing an acrid cloud of foul white smoke that, carried by the wind, can cover hundreds, or even thousands, of square miles.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To remove (items or material) so as to leave something unobstructed or open.

quote.citation: 1711 November 6, Joseph Addison, The Spectator, number 215:
quote.text: […]  Aristotle has brought to explain his Doctrine of Substantial Forms, when he tells us that a Statue lies hid in a Block of Marble; and that the Art of the statuary only clears away the superfluous Matter, and removes the Rubbish.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To leave abruptly; to clear off or clear out.

quote.citation: 1899 February, Joseph Conrad, “The Heart of Darkness”, in Blackwood’s Edinburgh Magazine, volume CLXV, number M, New York, N.Y.: The Leonard Scott Publishing Company, […], →OCLC, part I, page 199:
quote.text: Then the whole population cleared into the forest, expecting all kinds of calamities to happen, while, on the other hand, the steamer Fresleven commanded left also in a bad panic, in charge of the engineer, I believe.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To become free from obstruction or obscurement; to become transparent.
(transitive) To eliminate ambiguity or doubt from (a matter); to clarify or resolve; to clear up.
(transitive) To remove from suspicion, especially of having committed a crime.

quote.citation: 1713, John Dryden, “Preface”, in Fables Antient and Modern:
quote.text: […]  yet I appeal to the reader, and am sure he will clear me from Partiality.

quote.citation: 1713, Joseph Addison, Cato, a Tragedy, act III, scene v:
quote.text: How! Wouldst thou clear rebellion?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To pass without interference; to miss.
(transitive, activities such as jumping or throwing) To exceed a stated mark.
(transitive, video games) To finish or complete (a stage, challenge, or game).
(intransitive) Of a check or financial transaction, to go through as payment; to be processed so that the money is transferred.
(transitive, business) To earn a profit of; to net.

quote.citation: 1843, Thomas Babington Macaulay, The History of England from the Accession of James II‎[7], volume I, chapter V:
quote.text: The profit which she cleared on the cargo  […]  cannot be estimated at less than a thousand guineas.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To approve or authorise for a particular purpose or action; to give clearance to.
(transitive) To obtain approval or authorisation in respect of.
(intransitive) To obtain a clearance.
(transitive) To obtain permission to use (a sample of copyrighted audio) in another track.
To disengage oneself from incumbrances, distress, or entanglements; to become free.

quote.citation: 1613, Francis Bacon, The Eſſaies (second edition), essay 18: “Of Expences”:
quote.text: Beſides, he that cleares at once will relapſe: for finding himſelfe out of ſtraights, he will reuert to his cuſtomes. But hee that cleareth by degrees, induceth an habite of frugality, and gaineth as well vpon his minde, as vpon his Eſtate.

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive, sports) To hit, kick, head, punch etc. (a ball, puck) away in order to defend one's goal.

quote.citation: 2010 December 29, Chris Whyatt, “Chelsea 1-0 Bolton”, in BBC‎[8]:
quote.text: Bolton then went even closer when Elmander's cross was met by a bullet header from Holden, which forced a wonderful tip over from Cech before Drogba then cleared the resulting corner off the line.

definitions.definition: (transitive, computing) To reset or unset; to return to an empty state or to zero.
(transitive, computing) To style (an element within a document) so that it is not permitted to float at a given position.

quote.citation: 2010, Andy Harris, HTML, XHTML and CSS All-In-One For Dummies, page 290:
quote.text: To get the footer acting right, you need to float it and clear it on both margins.

definitions.definition: (transitive, firearms) To unload a firearm, or undergo an unloading procedure, in order to prevent negligent discharge; for safety reasons, to check whether one's firearm is loaded or unloaded.
(carpentry) Full extent; distance between extreme limits; especially; the distance between the nearest surfaces of two bodies, or the space between walls.
(video games) The completion of a stage or challenge, or of the whole game.
(Scientology) A person who is free from the influence of engrams.

quote.citation: 1985, Rodney Stark, William Sims Bainbridge, The Future of Religion, page 269:
quote.text: Today, clear status can be conferred only by high ranking ministers of the church, and clears are not presented for examination by outsiders.
